title: Harbor and Songbook
premise: Ada Sandoval, a cellist whose hands froze mid-concert and never quite recovered, retreats to the coastal town of Bellhaven to settle her late grandmother's orchard — only to discover the deed names a second heir: Jonah Reyes, the boy she loved at seventeen and abandoned when her career took off. Forced to share one stubborn piece of land through a single harvest season, they rebuild an uneasy partnership that deepens into something neither planned. When Ada's old orchestra offers a comeback tour timed against the final ferry of the season, she must choose between reclaiming the identity she lost on stage and the found family, the town, and Jonah who see her clearly now. She plays one last unannounced concert in the orchard itself, then boards nothing: she stays, co-founding a music school where the deed finally reads two names by choice.
about_author: Mirabel Quintana is the pen name of a former orchard bookkeeper who writes love stories set in small coastal towns where everyone knows your business before you do. Her novels center second chances, stubborn land, and the music people make when no one is grading them.

chapters.title: The Frozen Measure
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. A flashback frames the catastrophic final performance — her hands seizing mid-solo, the silence, the reviews — then cuts to Ada arriving in Bellhaven to handle her grandmother's estate. The emotional beat is grief disguised as efficiency; she treats the orchard as paperwork, not homecoming.

chapters.title: Two Names on One Deed
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. At the county office she discovers Jonah Reyes is co-heir of the orchard. He shows up at the property with a truckload of tools and eleven years of quiet resentment. The beat is collision: neither will sell, neither will leave, and the lawyer gives them one season to decide together.

chapters.title: Pruning Season
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Forced cooperation begins — pruning trees, arguing methods, trading barbed memories of the summer they split. Ada learns Jonah stayed to care for his ailing mother while she left for conservatory. The beat is reluctant respect taking root like the trees they're saving.

chapters.title: The Ferry Schedule
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Through Jonah's eyes we see Ada anew: the flinches at applause, the way she hums to the trees. Townsfolk fold her into harvest suppers and choir practice — a found family forming around her. The beat is tenderness he refuses to name, watching her belong somewhere new.

chapters.title: Cello in the Barn
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada finds her grandmother's old cello in the barn and, alone, plays for the first time since the collapse — badly, then honestly. Jonah overhears and doesn't applaud, just asks what she wants to play next. The beat is fragile reclamation: music without an audience might still be hers.

chapters.title: What the Letters Said
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. They find their grandmother and Jonah's mother were lifelong pen pals who engineered the shared deed deliberately, believing the orchard needed both families. Old letters reveal Ada's grandmother regretted pushing her toward the career. The beat is betrayal softening into understanding — the past was more complicated than blame.

chapters.title: First Frost, First Kiss
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Harvest festival night: lanterns, cider, a dance that isn't a dance until it is. They kiss under the first frost, then Ada pulls away, terrified of choosing anything after choosing wrong once. The beat is joy shadowed by fear — happiness feels like a debt coming due.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Her former conductor arrives with a comeback tour: principal cello, world stages, leaving on the last ferry in three weeks. It's everything she mourned, offered at exactly the wrong time. Jonah tells her to take it, meaning the opposite. The beat is rising tension — old ambition versus new love, loyalty versus truth about what she actually wants.

chapters.title: Last Ferry of the Season
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Ada packs, rehearses, and stands at the dock as the ferry loads — then walks the orchard instead and understands her hands never failed; her truth did. She calls the orchestra and declines. Jonah, told she'd gone, runs the shoreline road to find her among the trees. The beat is climax: the choice made, the confession spoken plainly at last.

chapters.title: Orchard Concerto
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, epilogue-adjacent. Spring: the deed amended to two willing names, the barn converted into a free community music school. Ada gives an unannounced concert between the apple rows for the whole town, hands steady, no reviews pending. The beat is resolution — identity rebuilt not as soloist or survivor, but as someone who stayed.
